summary: Describes the Generic Security Service API, a language-independent interface that lets applications use security services such as authentication without knowing which mechanism does the work. This update refines the earlier version 2 specification. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It is a universal plug for locks. Programs use one plug shape and any lock behind it can check who you are.

questions: how do applications use generic security services

subtitle: One programming interface that lets applications authenticate peers and protect messages without caring which security mechanism sits underneath.

tldr.problem: Every security technology, such as Kerberos or public-key schemes, has its own calls and data formats. An application written for one is stuck with it.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API defines a generic set of calls for credentials, security contexts and per-message protection. Opaque tokens carry the mechanism-specific details between the two peers.
tldr.outcome: This version 2, update 1 obsoletes RFC 2078 and is a Proposed Standard. It has since been updated by RFC 5554 and RFC 5896.

today: RFC 2743 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2078. It has been updated by RFC 5554 and RFC 5896, and the C language bindings are in RFC 2744.

sections.title: What GSS-API Is For
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) provides security services to callers in a generic fashion, supportable with a range of underlying mechanisms and technologies. The aim is source-level portability: an application can move to a different security environment without being rewritten.

A typical caller is itself a communications protocol. It asks GSS-API to protect its traffic with authentication, integrity and, optionally, confidentiality. The RFC defines services and primitives independently of any underlying mechanism and any programming language. Separate documents define language bindings and the token formats and procedures for each mechanism.

The design goals are mechanism independence, protocol environment independence, protocol association independence, and suitability to a range of implementation placements, inside or outside a system's Trusted Computing Base.
sections.eli5: Different locks need different keys. GSS-API lets a program say what it wants done and leaves the choice of lock to someone else.

sections.title: Credentials, Contexts and Tokens
sections.content:
A credential is what a peer needs before it can set up a security context. Callers refer to credentials through handles, so they never touch the credential contents. Passing GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL asks for the default principal, and the RFC spells out how a default is chosen for initiators and for acceptors.

Two peers build a security context by exchanging tokens. Context-level tokens set up and manage the context. Per-message tokens protect individual data messages on an established context. Token contents are opaque to the caller, who just carries them to the peer. The first context-level token must begin with an Object Identifier naming the mechanism.

The API is independent of the transport. The caller decides how to ship tokens, in-band or out-of-band, and must tell token types apart. Several contexts can exist at once between the same two peers, which allows graceful rollover when credentials expire.

The RFC also describes channel bindings. These are caller-supplied data about the underlying channel, such as addresses. They limit where an intercepted context establishment token could be reused by an attacker. Using them is a caller option.
sections.eli5: A credential is your ID card, a context is a private phone line you and a friend set up, and tokens are the notes you pass back and forth while setting it up.

sections.title: Names
sections.content:
GSS-API treats names as opaque objects, because different mechanisms authenticate names in different forms. It defines three kinds of representation: an internal name that only the implementation understands, a flat octet string tagged with an OID that says which namespace it belongs to, and an Exported Name Object.

A Mechanism Name (MN) is an internal name tied to exactly one mechanism. Portable calls handle names for the caller: GSS_Import_name(), GSS_Display_name(), GSS_Compare_name(), GSS_Release_name() and GSS_Duplicate_name(). Callers should not compare printable names themselves. They should use GSS_Compare_name().

For large access control lists, GSS_Export_name() turns an MN into a flat name that can be compared directly, for example with memcmp(). It carries a header with the OID of the authenticating mechanism and a trailer with the name. Section 4 also defines name types, such as the host-based service form service@hostname and an anonymous name type.
sections.eli5: Names are like name tags that say which club they came from. GSS-API lets programs check whether two tags match without reading the fine print on each one.

sections.title: Setting Up a Context and Sending a Message
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a typical exchange. The client calls GSS_Init_sec_context() with the target name and asks for mutual authentication. The call returns an output token and the status GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED. The client sends the token to the server.

The server passes it to GSS_Accept_sec_context(). This returns GSS_S_COMPLETE, the client's authenticated identity in src_name, and a token for the client. The client feeds that token into a second GSS_Init_sec_context() call, which completes mutual authentication.

Now the client calls GSS_Wrap() to apply data origin authentication, integrity and, optionally, confidentiality, and sends the result. The server calls GSS_Unwrap() to reverse it and check it. When done, GSS_Delete_sec_context() frees the context, and may produce a token telling the peer to do the same.

The GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED status lets mechanisms with more round trips use the same calling pattern, so applications need no separate code path for each one. The RFC also notes that no initialization call exists, so implementations must be self-initializing.
sections.eli5: You knock, the other side answers to prove who they are, and only then do you start passing sealed envelopes back and forth.

sections.title: Optional Services and Message Protection
sections.content:
An initiator asks for optional services by setting flags in req_flags on GSS_Init_sec_context(). The defined services are delegation, mutual authentication, replay detection, out-of-sequence detection, anonymous authentication, and availability of per-message confidentiality and integrity. A mechanism that cannot provide a requested service should proceed without it. The application learns what it got from the ret_flags output and can abort if the service was mandatory.

Per-message calls come in two pairs. GSS_GetMIC() and GSS_VerifyMIC() give integrity and data origin authentication. GSS_Wrap() and GSS_Unwrap() add optional confidentiality. When replay detection is on, a message can be flagged as GSS_S_DUPLICATE_TOKEN or GSS_S_OLD_TOKEN. With sequencing on, GSS_S_UNSEQ_TOKEN and GSS_S_GAP_TOKEN can appear. Detection does not stop a suspect message from reaching the recipient, so policy is up to the caller.

Other features include a quality-of-protection (QOP) parameter, where most callers use the default. An anonymity request is not binding on the mechanism, but the caller is told whether it was honored. Delegation lets the acceptor act as an agent of the initiator, and it only happens if the application asks. GSS_Export_sec_context() and GSS_Import_sec_context() move a context between processes on one machine.
sections.eli5: When you start a call you can ask for extras, like a lock on the envelope or a count of every note. Some phone lines cannot do all of them, so you check what you really got.

sections.title: Status Reporting
sections.content:
Every call returns two status values. major_status is mechanism independent and drives normal control flow. minor_status carries mechanism-specific detail, and its values are not specified in this document.

Major status codes split into fatal errors and informatory codes. Fatal examples are GSS_S_BAD_MECH for an unsupported mechanism, GSS_S_BAD_NAME for an invalid name, GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN, GSS_S_NO_CRED and GSS_S_FAILURE. Informatory codes include GSS_S_COMPLETE, GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and the four sequencing codes. During context establishment, sequencing codes appear only with GSS_S_FAILURE, so they are always fatal there.

Local status cannot reflect unpredictable events at a remote peer, because no GSS-API call waits on a serialized interaction with the peer. Passing remote problems along is the caller's job. The RFC also recommends robust behavior: failing calls free their memory, one failed call should not ruin the context, and GSS_Delete_sec_context() should keep working whenever possible.
sections.eli5: Each call answers with a plain result, like a green or red light, plus a note with the fine details. The light tells your program what to do next.

sections.title: The Mechanism-Independent Token Tag
sections.content:
Section 3.1 defines a tag for the first token of a context establishment sequence, so a receiver can tell which mechanism it belongs to. Internet standards-track GSS-API mechanisms are required to use it for initial tokens. Using it for later tokens is optional.

The tag is defined in octets, though derived from ASN.1 and DER. This lets implementers avoid general ASN.1 code. It consists, in order, of: the byte 0x60, a length field, the byte 0x06 for an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, the OID length, and the OID octets. Lengths under 128 use one octet. Larger lengths use a first octet with the high bit set, giving the count of following octets, then the value.

The mechanism-defined token follows immediately, with no separate size field after the OID. Examples given for mechanism OIDs are the Kerberos V5 mechanism, 1.2.840.113554.1.2.2, and the DASS mechanism, 1.3.12.2.1011.7.5.
sections.eli5: The first note carries a label saying which secret language the rest is written in. That way the receiver knows which decoder to pick up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that using the interface does not by itself provide security services or assurance. Those depend on the underlying mechanisms. Callers must pay attention to the requests they make and the status indicators they get back, because those describe the protection actually in effect.

Inter-process tokens made by GSS_Export_sec_context() may contain sensitive data, including cryptographic keys. Applications must protect them in transit and apply local controls to limit access. The robustness advice and credential-handling notes apply too: the ability to use a principal's credentials is equivalent to the ability to assert that principal's identity, so the system below GSS-API must restrict access to credentials.
sections.eli5: The plug does not make the lock strong. Strength comes from the lock behind it, so watch the signals it gives you.

messages.note: Status is GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED because mutual authentication was requested.

messages.note: Server status is GSS_S_COMPLETE and src_name holds the client identity.

viz.caption: OPTIONAL SERVICES AN INITIATOR CAN REQUEST

items.title: Delegation
items.text: Lets the acceptor act as an agent of the initiator.

items.title: Mutual authentication
items.text: The acceptor also proves its identity to the initiator.

items.title: Out-of-sequence detection
items.text: Flags messages received out of order.

items.title: Anonymous authentication
items.text: Does not reveal the initiator's identity to the acceptor.

items.title: Per-message confidentiality and integrity
items.text: Asks that these protections be available on the context.
